section.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth
section.sectionRationale: Revelation 21:1-8 opens the seventh and final vision cycle of the book. After the judgment of Babylon, the beast, the false prophet, and the devil in chapters 19-20, the scene turns at last to God's own dwelling with His people. This unit is a self-contained overture, a declaration straight from the throne, that stands before the angel's detailed, guided tour of the New Jerusalem begins in 21:9-22:5. It closes with a stark either/or, overcomers who inherit all things and the unrepentant who face the second death, marking a clean seam before the next section's extended vision of the bride city.
section.thesis: The dwelling of God with man, promised since Eden and pictured in the tabernacle, is here declared complete: the old order of death, mourning, and pain passes away, all things are made new, and every reader is confronted with the choice between overcoming faith and the second death.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the new heaven and new earth with the holy city descending like a bride; the voice from the throne announcing that God's dwelling is now with man; the enthroned One's declaration, 'Behold, I make all things new,' and His self-naming as the Alpha and the Omega; and the closing contrast between the one who overcomes and those who are shut out into the second death.

units.label: A new heaven and a new earth

verses.text: Then I saw a {{kainos|new}} heaven and a {{kainos|new}} earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.
I saw the holy city, the {{kainos|new}} Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the {{skenoo|dwelling place}} of God is with man, and He will {{skenoo|dwell}} with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.
‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.”

units.label: Behold, I make all things new

verses.text: And the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things {{kainos|new}}.” Then He said, “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.”
And He told me, “It is done! I am the {{alpha_omega|Alpha and the Omega}}, the Beginning and the End. To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life.
The one who {{nikao|overcomes}} will inherit all things, and I will be his God, and he will be My son.

But to the cowardly and unbelieving and abominable and murderers and sexually immoral and sorcerers and idolaters and all liars, their place will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur. This is the second death.”

kainos.gloss: New in kind or quality, as distinct from neos, new merely in time. The new heaven, new earth, and new Jerusalem are not simply young; they are a fresh, transformed order altogether. The same word governs the throne's own declaration, 'Behold, I make all things new.'

skenoo.gloss: To tabernacle or dwell, drawn from skene, a tent. It recalls the tabernacle where God dwelt among Israel behind a veil, Exodus 25:8, and the Word who 'tabernacled' among us, John 1:14. Here the dwelling is at last permanent, direct, and unveiled.

alpha_omega.gloss: The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, a title of eternity and total sovereignty over history from its beginning to its end. God takes this title for Himself here, and the risen Christ takes the identical title in Revelation 1:8, 1:17, and 22:13.

nikao.gloss: To conquer or overcome. It is the repeated call to the seven churches in Revelation 2-3, and here it names the one who perseveres in faith in Christ rather than joining the list of verse 8. To overcome is not sinless perfection but persevering trust in the Lamb who has already conquered.

basic.context: After Babylon and the beast are judged, John sees the goal of the whole story: a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city coming down like a bride. A voice from the throne announces that God will now live with His people directly, with no more death, tears, or pain.
basic.hermeneutics: Most readers take this as a real, future, physical hope, though they debate whether it is this creation renewed or an entirely fresh creation. Either way, the passage is a promise to be received in hope, and its one command to the reader is to overcome rather than to shrink back.
basic.originalLanguages: The word for 'new,' kainos, means new in quality, not just new in time. God will 'tabernacle,' skenoo, with His people, unveiled at last. He calls Himself the Alpha and the Omega, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and promises that 'the one who overcomes,' using the same Greek word, nikao, found throughout Revelation, will inherit all things.
basic.typology: This is the direct answer to Genesis 3, where God's presence withdrew and a flaming sword barred the way back to the tree of life. Here God Himself comes to dwell with man without any barrier at all, and the tabernacle's veiled presence among Israel becomes an unveiled, permanent dwelling.
basic.christ: The One who says 'It is done' and takes the title Alpha and Omega is Christ, who said 'It is finished' on the cross and takes this very title again in Revelation 22:13. His finished work secures both salvation and this new creation.
basic.god: God is the one who at last dwells with His people without distance, faithful and true to His own promises, sovereign to make all things new, and just, drawing a clear line between those who overcome and those who do not.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 65:17 promises new heavens and a new earth. Isaiah 25:8 promises God will wipe away every tear, quoted almost exactly here. Ezekiel 37:27 promises God's dwelling among His people. Genesis 3:24 is the exile this passage reverses.
basic.oneStory: Genesis 3 ended with humanity driven out and a flaming sword guarding the tree of life. Revelation 21 begins the answer: God Himself comes down to dwell with His people forever, wiping away the very tears that began in the garden, and making all things new.

context.literary:
Revelation 21:1-8 is built as three speeches in one breath. Verses 1 and 2 are seen, each opening with 'I saw.' Verses 3 and 4 are heard, 'I heard a loud voice.' Verses 5 to 8 are spoken by a third voice, the One seated on the throne, and nothing else in the book is quite like it. Almost all of Revelation reaches John through angels, through Christ, or through the Spirit. The Father Himself is heard in the first person only here and at Revelation 1:8, so the opening and the closing movements of the book are framed by the same voice and the same title, the Alpha and the Omega.

The unit is held together by a frame of passing away. 'The first heaven and earth had passed away,' verse 1, is answered by 'the former things have passed away,' verse 4, and between them sit five negatives, no sea, no death, no mourning, no crying, no pain. The centre is the sentence nobody else in the passage can say, 'Behold, I make all things new,' verse 5. The voice then turns from announcement to invitation, the thirsty drinking freely in verse 6, and from invitation to a fork in verses 7 and 8, the one who overcomes and the list of those outside.

The passage also answers its immediate past. Revelation 20:11-15 closed with earth and heaven fleeing from the great white throne, the sea giving up its dead, and the lake of fire called 'the second death.' Chapter 21 opens where the old creation is gone and repeats the phrase 'second death' in verse 8, so that the reader hears the same judgment as the edge of the new world rather than its content. Verse 9 then begins a deliberate mirror of Revelation 17:1. The same sort of angel, one of the seven with the bowls, shows John a woman in each case, the great prostitute and the bride. The book is built as a tale of two cities and two women, and chapter 21 is the second panel.
context.historical:
John writes from Patmos, an island, and the sea was the thing that cut him off from the churches he served. For the first hearers the sea was also the place where empires arrived. Rome's fleets and merchants came by water, and Revelation 18 will count the ships and the cargoes of Babylon's trade. In the Old Testament the sea is the realm of chaos that God restrains, and Daniel 7:2-3 has the beasts rise out of it, as the beast of Revelation 13:1 does. To say 'the sea was no more' was to promise believers who lived under pressure that the source of the threat itself would not exist.

These churches were small, mostly poor, and watching neighbours get ahead by joining in the civic cult of the emperor. Rome called itself the eternal city, and its poets spoke of an empire without end. John answers with a city that really does last, one that comes from God rather than from the legions. The martyrs of Revelation 6:9-11 had asked 'How long, O Lord?' and had been given a white robe and told to wait. The wiping away of tears in 21:4 is the answer to that waiting.

The picture of a bride and groom drew on weddings every hearer knew. The bridegroom came for his bride, she was adorned for him, and the two households met in a celebration. Isaiah had already used the image of a city dressed for marriage, Isaiah 62:5. Jewish hope in the centuries between the Testaments also looked for a renewed heaven and earth, so the idea was not strange. What was new was the claim that it had been secured by a slain Lamb, and that the seer saw it as already certain enough to call 'done.'
context.canonical:
The language of this passage is a tapestry of earlier promises, and the footnote in the BSB directs readers to Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 for the new heaven and earth. In Isaiah 65:17-19 God says, 'I will create new heavens and a new earth,' and a Jerusalem in which 'the sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard.' Isaiah 66:22 adds that the new heavens and earth will 'endure before Me,' so that the name and the descendants of God's people endure with them. The tears of verse 4 come from Isaiah 25:8, where the Lord God 'will swallow up death forever' and 'wipe away the tears from every face.' John had already used the same line at Revelation 7:17.

The voice of verse 3 gathers the covenant promise that runs from the wilderness to the exile. 'I will make My dwelling place among you,' Leviticus 26:11-12, 'I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God,' Exodus 29:45, and Ezekiel's 'My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people,' Ezekiel 37:27, all arrive here with the barrier removed. The Gospel of John had said that the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and Paul told the Corinthians that they are already the temple of the living God, 2 Corinthians 6:16, so this verse is the end of a long road.

The overcomer of verse 7 is the figure of Revelation 2 and 3. Each letter to the churches ended with a promise, among them the tree of life, Revelation 2:7, no harm from the second death, 2:11, and a place on Christ's throne, 3:21. Verse 7 gathers them into one: 'will inherit all things.' Verse 7 also borrows the words God spoke to David about his son, 'I will be his Father, and he will be My son,' 2 Samuel 7:14, and hands them to every believer. Peter's 'new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells,' 2 Peter 3:13, and Paul's creation set free, Romans 8:19-21, are the New Testament echoes.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John was writing to churches that were being told, in ten thousand small ways, that the Roman world was the real world and that faithfulness to Christ was a costly eccentricity. He gives them the end of the story first, so that they can read their own present in its light. The new creation is the verdict on every claim that power, wealth or fear is the last word.

He also meant to tell them what the end is. It is not an escape from the creation into something merely spiritual, and not a quiet retirement. It is a city descending to earth, God coming down to live with a people who have been wiped clean of tears. John stresses that this world is the Lord's own project, and that He finishes what He begins, which is why the voice says 'It is done.'

The fork in verses 7 and 8 is not an afterthought. John wants hearers who are tempted to compromise, the cowardly who would deny Christ under pressure, to see the weight of what they would be trading. The promise and the warning are given to the same people in the same breath, so that the promise strengthens them to stand and the warning keeps them from drifting.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is almost wholly description, and the main danger is turning it into a calendar or a blueprint. Nothing here tells believers to build a perfect society, to wait for the physical world to fail, or to treat the present creation as disposable. The hope of a renewed world is meant to sustain faithful work in the present one, as Paul's argument in Romans 8:19-23 suggests, rather than to excuse neglect of it.

The command that does hide in the passage is the call to overcome. Revelation tells us how that is done, 'by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony,' Revelation 12:11, not by force or self-effort. The list of verse 8 is likewise a description of the people who finally refuse God, not a set of tests for tracking down who is in or out. It is meant to keep every reader honest about where their own loyalty lies and to send the thirsty to the free water of verse 6.

debates.question: Does 'a new heaven and a new earth' mean this creation renewed, or the old one ended and replaced?

views.label: Renewal of this creation
views.case: The Greek word is kainos, new in kind, not neos, new in time. Romans 8:19-21 pictures the creation itself set free from its bondage to decay, not thrown away, and 1 Corinthians 15 teaches a body that is transformed rather than swapped. Peter's flood language in 2 Peter 3:6 speaks of the world being 'destroyed' by water, and yet the earth plainly continued, which suggests that 'destroyed' there means purged, not annihilated. Many Reformed and Lutheran writers read the passage this way.

views.label: A wholly new act of creation
views.case: 2 Peter 3:10-13 speaks of the heavens disappearing with a roar and the elements destroyed by fire, and Revelation 20:11 says that earth and heaven fled and 'no place was found for them.' On this view the language of verse 1, 'passed away,' is stronger than renovation, and the weight falls on God creating afresh, as He first made all things from nothing.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that the result is a real, physical, everlasting home. The two texts that seem to pull apart, Romans 8 and 2 Peter 3, can each be heard as describing a fire that refines and a freedom that follows. The question affects how much weight to put on the present creation's goodness, but not on the certainty of the promise.

debates.question: Is the list of verse 8 a warning to believers or a description of unbelievers?

views.label: A description of those who finally reject God
views.case: The list begins with 'the cowardly' and 'the unbelieving' and ends with 'all liars.' It describes people whose lives are marked by these things, and it closely matches the exclusion lists of 21:27 and 22:15, which name those outside the city. On this reading John is describing the character of the finally unrepentant.

views.label: A warning that includes professing Christians
views.case: The letters to the seven churches warn believers that those who do not overcome can lose their place, Revelation 2:5 and 3:5, and the first group named in verse 8, the cowardly, are exactly the people who would shrink back under persecution. On this view the list is a real warning to the church to hold fast, as Hebrews 10:38-39 also pleads.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: Some hold that the list describes the finally lost and also functions as a warning to everyone within earshot, because real faith endures. Those who read it this way point to Revelation 3:5, where the one who overcomes is promised that his name will never be blotted out.

debates.bearing: However the weight is spread, verse 6 sets an open hand beside the list. The water is free to the thirsty, so the warning is meant to drive people to the spring, not away from it, and the church is told to hold on rather than to count heads.

study.originalLanguages:
The first heaven and earth 'had passed away,' verse 1, uses an aorist verb, apelthan, literally 'went away.' John speaks as though the old order has already gone, and the same tense and the same verb come back in verse 4, 'the former things have passed away.' The two uses fence in the section, and the repeated aorist makes the future event feel finished from the standpoint of the vision.

The words 'It is done' in verse 6 translate a single Greek verb, gegonan, a perfect tense of ginomai, 'to come about.' The perfect describes a completed event whose results stand. The verb is plural, 'they have come to pass,' so the BSB's 'It is done' gathers up all the things the book has promised. In the same breath verse 5 uses a present tense, 'I make all things new,' literally 'I am making.' God speaks as one who is at work now and has finished in the end, a pairing the English cannot easily hold.

The wiping of the tears in verse 4 uses the verb exaleipho, 'to wipe away, to blot out.' The same verb is used of sins that are wiped out, Acts 3:19 and Colossians 2:14, and of names that are not blotted out of the Book of Life, Revelation 3:5. The comfort of the verse is not only that grief is soothed but that its cause is erased. In verse 3, many Greek manuscripts read the plural 'peoples,' laoi, instead of 'His people,' so that God dwells with a gathered humanity of many nations, as Revelation 7:9 pictures.

The 'free' gift of the spring in verse 6 translates dorean, 'as a gift.' Paul uses it for the justification believers receive 'freely by His grace,' Romans 3:24. The adverb stands in deliberate tension with the verb of verse 7, 'overcomes,' and with the warning of verse 8, and the passage holds both: the water is given and the one who drinks is expected to hold on. In verse 7 the word for 'inherit,' kleronomeo, is the word of sonship and family property, and the promise that follows borrows the words of 2 Samuel 7:14 about David's son, 'I will be his Father, and he will be My son.' The royal promise has become the portion of every overcomer.

The first item in the list of verse 8 is deilois, 'the cowardly,' the fearful. It stands at the head, and perhaps for a reason. The book is addressed to people who might be afraid, and John lists the cowardly before the murderers, before the idolaters, and before the liars, so that the fear that makes believers shrink back is named as a serious danger.

typology.type: The tabernacle and the dwelling of God, Exodus 25:8
typology.fulfillment: God told Israel to build a sanctuary 'so that I may dwell among them,' Exodus 25:8, and the tent was a place of curtains, priests and limits. John 1:14 says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' using the same root as the 'dwelling place' of verse 3. The escalation is complete here, since the dwelling is no longer a tent in the middle of a camp but a whole renewed creation with God in it. The type falls short in that Israel could approach only through blood and priests, Hebrews 9:7-8, while the new creation has no curtain at all.

The world opened with God walking in a garden, Genesis 3:8, and a tree of life guarded by cherubim after the fall, Genesis 3:24. Revelation 21:6 offers free water of life to the thirsty, and chapter 22 will show the tree again. The correspondence is deliberate, and so is the escalation: Eden was a garden and the final place is a city, a place where human culture is kept and gathered. The type falls short because Adam could still fall. Verse 7 speaks of an inheritance that cannot be forfeited.

typology.type: The sea and the waters of chaos, Genesis 1:2
typology.fulfillment: At the creation the Spirit hovered over the waters and God gathered them into seas, Genesis 1:2 and 1:9-10. In the Old Testament the sea becomes the place of threat, the flood, the Egyptian army and the home of Leviathan. In Revelation the beast rises from the sea, 13:1, and the sea gives up its dead at the judgment, 20:13. The words 'the sea was no more' announce that what threatened the creation is finally gone. The type is not a command to fear water, since the same Bible calls the seas good, Genesis 1:10, but it names the chaos that the Lamb has conquered.

typology.type: The bride and the marriage of God to His people, Isaiah 62:5
typology.fulfillment: The prophets spoke of God as the bridegroom of Israel, Isaiah 62:5 and Hosea 2:19-20, and Paul teaches that Christ gave Himself up for the church 'to present her to Himself as a glorious church,' Ephesians 5:25-27. In Revelation 19:7-8 the bride has made herself ready and has been given fine linen, and here she appears as the city. The type goes beyond Israel's marriage in that the bride is made spotless by the bridegroom's own work rather than by her own faithfulness. It also falls short of ordinary marriage, which ends at death, while this union does not, verse 4.

typology.type: The inheritance of the land, and sonship, 2 Samuel 7:14
typology.fulfillment: Israel was brought in to inherit a land, and David's son was promised God's fatherhood in 2 Samuel 7:14. Verse 7 hands both promises to the one who overcomes: 'will inherit all things,' and 'he will be My son.' Paul calls believers 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17. The escalation is from a strip of land to the whole renewed creation, and from one king's son to every believer. The type falls short in that the land could be lost to exile, but this inheritance is held by the One who says, 'It is done.'

study.christ:
The throne speaks in verses 5 to 8, and in this book the throne is never the Father's alone. Revelation 22:1 and 22:3 speak of 'the throne of God and of the Lamb,' a single throne, and 3:21 has Christ saying that He 'sat down with My Father on His throne.' When the One seated on the throne takes the title 'the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End,' the book has already used the matching title for Christ in 1:17, 'the First and the Last,' and 2:8, 'who died and returned to life,' which are Isaiah's own words for the LORD, Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12. John does not set the Father and the Son against each other in this vision. He lets one throne and one set of titles carry both, and this is why the church read the book as a testimony to the deity of Christ.

The promise of the water points the same way. In verse 6 God offers 'the spring of the water of life' to the thirsty, and the Gospel of John records Jesus calling out at the feast, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37, and promising the Samaritan woman water that becomes a spring in the one who drinks. Isaiah 55:1 had invited 'all you who are thirsty, come to the waters.' The invitation of Isaiah, of Jesus and of Revelation 21:6 is a single invitation made by the one Lord.

The new creation is also the work of Christ. Paul says that through Him God reconciles 'all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven,' Colossians 1:20, and that God's plan is 'to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ,' Ephesians 1:10. Christ is 'the firstfruits' of the resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and Paul says the last enemy, death, will be destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:26. Revelation 21:4 is the moment when that enemy is gone for good. The overcomers are people who follow the one who overcame first, as Revelation 3:21 says, 'just as I overcame.' Even the title 'son' in verse 7 means that believers share in the sonship of the Son, Romans 8:17.

Caution is wise. The passage does not mention the cross by name, and a reader should not invent a hidden Christ in every detail. The Lamb appears in the verses that follow, and the connection with His death is made elsewhere in the book, as when the book of life is called the Lamb's, Revelation 13:8 and 21:27. What this passage gives is the destination that His work secures, and the voice that guarantees it.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He is the one who acts and who has the last word. The book of Revelation has been full of the voices of angels, beasts, martyrs and kings, and here the One seated on the throne speaks for Himself and says, 'Behold, I make all things new.' Everything depends on Him: the descent of the city, the end of death, the opening of the water. The vision shows no negotiation, because the God who made the first creation is under no obligation to anyone to make the second.

He is a God who comes down. The movement of the whole passage is from heaven to earth, the city 'coming down out of heaven,' the voice saying that His dwelling place 'is with man.' This corrects every picture of salvation as a flight from matter to a distant sky. God's intention for His creatures was always to live among them, and the first chapters of Genesis show Him walking in the garden. The end of the story returns to the beginning of the story, but with the road to ruin closed.

He is tender. The detail of verse 4 is startling in a book full of thunder: God wipes away the tears Himself. A God who made the stars attends to the faces of people who have wept. That sets the vast scale of the new creation beside a very small and personal scene.

He is faithful and true, as He says of His own words in verse 5, and the pairing of 'faithful' and 'true' is the pairing used of Christ in Revelation 19:11. The God who promised Abraham, Moses, David and Isaiah is keeping His word to the last detail, and the phrase 'It is done' is His own signature on all of it.

He is also just, and the passage does not look away from this. The same voice that gives freely to the thirsty names a second death in verse 8, for those who have refused Him. His holiness does not make Him less kind, nor His kindness less holy. For worship, the passage teaches believers to sing as people who know how the story ends, to take their grief to the God who will wipe it away, and to treat the free invitation of verse 6 as something to accept now rather than later.

crossReferences.note: The promise that stands behind verse 1. God says He will create new heavens and a new earth and a Jerusalem that is a joy, where weeping and crying will no longer be heard. John takes the whole picture and shows it arriving, with the weeping of verse 4 answering the weeping of Isaiah.

Isaiah adds that the new heavens and the new earth 'will endure before Me,' and that God's people and their name will endure with them. The BSB footnote on Revelation 21:1 sends the reader to this verse, and it shows that John's new creation is a lasting home for the people of God.

The source of the tears in verse 4. Isaiah says the Lord God will swallow up death forever and wipe away the tears from every face. John has already quoted it at 7:17, and here it comes to its full realisation, since death itself is now no more.

At the foot of Sinai God promised, 'I will make My dwelling place among you,' and 'I will walk among you and be your God.' The covenant formula of verse 3 is the same, and the promise Israel could only taste in the tabernacle is given its final form.

Ezekiel promises an everlasting covenant of peace and a sanctuary set among the people forever, with the words 'My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people.' Revelation 21:3 almost repeats it, showing how the exilic promise reaches its goal.

The Word 'made His dwelling among us,' using the same verb root as the 'dwelling place' of Revelation 21:3. The incarnation was the first step in God's coming to live with people, and the new creation is the last step.

Paul says the creation was subjected to futility in hope and will be set free from bondage to decay. The new heaven and earth are the answer to that groaning, and the passage supports the reading in which the creation itself is renewed and not merely replaced.

Peter describes the Day of the Lord with fire and the disappearing of the heavens, and then says 'we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.' The two passages describe the same hope, and Peter ties it to how believers should live now.

God banished the man and stationed cherubim and a whirling sword to guard the way to the tree of life. Revelation 21 is the reversal of this exile: the barrier is gone, the water of life is offered freely, and the people live where God lives.

An earlier picture of the same hope for the multitude before the throne. God spreads His tabernacle over them, they never hunger or thirst, and He wipes away every tear. The two scenes belong together, and chapter 21 reveals that what the martyrs glimpsed in heaven becomes the world.

The judgment that comes immediately before this chapter. Earth and heaven flee, the dead are judged, and death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, called the second death. Chapter 21 stands on the far side of that judgment, which is why verse 4 can say that death is no more.

Christ promises the overcomer a seat on His throne, 'just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne.' It shows what 'overcomes' in 21:7 means and to whom it points, since the overcomer follows the pattern that Christ first set.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a creation described as very good and a Creator who walks in it, and it ends with the same two things restored. Between them stands a fall that told the story of every later grief. This passage is the point at which the whole line is drawn together, and it answers several questions the Bible had left open. Where did the dwelling of God go when Eden closed? Into a tent, then a temple, then a human body, and now into the whole of a new world. What became of the promise to Abraham of an inheritance? It becomes the whole earth, and verse 7 hands the promise to anyone who overcomes. What of the long wait of the martyrs, Revelation 6:10? It is met by a God who personally wipes away the tears.

The passage also looks back to the beginning in its details. The sea that was gathered at creation, Genesis 1:9-10, and that became the home of the beast, is gone. The tree of life of Genesis 2:9 is not named in this section, but the offer of free water carries Eden forward, and chapter 22 will put the tree back where it belongs. The curse spoken in Genesis 3 is the real subject of the five negatives in verse 4.

It sets up what follows. The angel will carry John away in verse 9 to see the bride in detail, a city of gold and jewels with no temple and no night, and the epilogue of 22:6-21 will hold open the invitation, 'Come,' to the thirsty. The one who overcomes in verse 7 will be shown to be a citizen of the city, and the cowardly and the liars will be kept outside.

It ends the story as a new creation, not a retirement. God is not merely saving souls out of the world. He is making the whole world new, and the gathered people will live in it and be at home with their God. This is the thing Genesis 1 and 2 were pointing toward and what Genesis 3 had broken, and it is the thing the apostles meant when they spoke of the renewal of all things, Matthew 19:28.

sermon.title: The New Heaven and New Earth
sermon.why: Preached on Revelation 21:1-7 in the series Bible: The Whole Story, Keller shows how the resurrection of Christ is the first installment of the new heaven and new earth, giving suffering believers a living hope rather than an abstract idea.

quiz.q: What does John see pass away in Revelation 21:1?

options.text: The first heaven and the first earth, along with the sea, replaced by a new heaven and a new earth.
options.note: This is the plain statement of verse 1.

options.text: Only the sea, while heaven and earth continue unchanged.
options.note: The sea's passing is notable, but the first heaven and earth themselves are also said to have passed away.

options.text: Only sinful people, while creation itself stays exactly the same.
options.note: The text describes a change in creation itself, not merely in people.

options.text: Nothing; the vision describes no real change at all.
options.note: The whole vision turns on decisive change, a new heaven and a new earth.

quiz.q: What does the loud voice from the throne declare in verse 3?

options.text: That the dwelling place of God is now with man, and He will be their God and they His people.
options.note: This is the Immanuel promise stated directly.

options.text: That the temple in Jerusalem would soon be rebuilt.
options.note: The vision actually moves away from a localized temple; see Revelation 21:22.

options.text: That God would visit His people occasionally from now on.
options.note: The promise is continual, unbroken dwelling, not occasional visits.

options.text: That God remains distant from His people forever.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the voice declares.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by calling Himself the Alpha and the Omega in verse 6?

options.text: That He is the beginning and end of all things, eternal and sovereign over the whole of history.
options.note: Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, a title of eternity.

options.text: That He is merely the first among many gods.
options.note: This misreads the monotheistic force of the title within Revelation's vision of the one true God.

options.text: That He created only the beginning of the world, not its end.
options.note: The title claims both the beginning and the end, not one without the other.

options.text: That the title belongs to an angel rather than to God or Christ.
options.note: The title is claimed by the One on the throne, and by Christ Himself in Revelation 22:13.

quiz.q: What does it mean to 'overcome' in verse 7?

options.text: To hold fast to Christ in persevering faith rather than falling into the sins listed in verse 8.
options.note: This matches the repeated call to overcome addressed to the churches in Revelation 2-3.

options.text: To achieve moral perfection entirely through personal effort.
options.note: Overcoming is persevering faith in Christ, who gives freely from the spring of life, not bare self-effort.

options.text: To defeat other people in worldly conflict.
options.note: This is not the sense of the word in Revelation's letters to the churches.

options.text: To avoid ever facing any hardship in this life.
options.note: Revelation is written precisely to strengthen believers facing hardship, not to promise its absence.

quiz.q: What is the 'second death' named in verse 8?

options.text: Final, eternal exclusion from God's presence in the lake of fire, distinct from ordinary bodily death.
options.note: Revelation names this same second death in 2:11 and 20:6, 14.

options.text: Simply another term for ordinary physical death.
options.note: Revelation distinguishes the second death as a further, final judgment beyond bodily death.

options.text: A temporary punishment after which everyone is restored.
options.note: This softens the stark, final warning language of the passage.

options.text: A blessing promised to those who overcome.
options.note: This is the opposite; the second death is the warning given to the unrepentant, not a reward.

questions: God's own dwelling with His people is the goal of the whole Bible, from Eden to here. Where do you most need to know that God is near, not distant, right now?
Verse 4 promises no more tears, mourning, crying, or pain, the very griefs Genesis 3 introduced into the world. What sorrow are you carrying that this promise speaks directly to?
The Alpha and Omega offers the water of life freely to the thirsty. What are you tempted to work for or earn instead of simply receiving it as a gift?
Overcomers inherit all things by continuing to trust Christ, not by sinless perfection. Where do you need courage to keep trusting rather than shrink back this week?
The list in verse 8 is sobering. Are there patterns there, even in small ways, that God may be calling you to repent of and leave behind?

translationNotes.note: New, kainos, describes newness in kind or quality, not merely in time, neos; much of the debate over renewal versus replacement of creation turns on this distinction.
The Greek verb skenoo, to dwell or tabernacle, recalls the tabernacle where God dwelt among Israel behind a veil, Exodus 25:8; here the dwelling is direct and unmediated.
Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, a title of eternity and sovereignty that Christ takes again for Himself in Revelation 22:13.
The 'second death' is a phrase unique to Revelation, see also 2:11 and 20:6, 14, naming a final judgment beyond ordinary bodily death.

meta.notes: BSB text supplied and pre-verified this session; Poetic line breaks were already flattened into flowing prose as supplied. Straight quotation marks were converted to curly typographic marks, and the continuous divine speech running from verse 3 into verse 4, and from verse 6 into verse 8, was punctuated as a single closed quotation to match standard BSB rendering; no wording was altered.
